title: Hola Mohalla
hook: at Anandpur, the day after Holi, mock battles, gatka and poetry fill the fields

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bandi Chhor, the Guru who freed the fifty-two. Your line was light for the freed. Today, a field full of horses.

A wide field in March. The day before, much of north India played Holi: colored powder everywhere, everyone pink and green and laughing. The next morning, at Anandpur Sahib in Punjab, something else begins. Horses thunder across the open ground. A rider in a tall blue turban stands on two galloping horses at once. Pairs face off with sticks and small shields, spinning, blocking, grinning. Somewhere a poet recites to a crowd. Somewhere else a langar feeds everyone who turns up. It's loud, dusty and joyful. It's Hola Mohalla.
screen: `HOLI, THE DAY BEFORE.` → `HORSES, STICKS AND SHIELDS.` → `A POET, A LANGAR, A CROWD.`

segments.voice: Hola Mohalla goes back to Guru Gobind Singh. Tradition says that around 1701, at Anandpur, he called the Sikhs together the day after Holi, not for colored powder but for drills and mock battles. The name is explained more than one way. Hola is often linked to Holi, and also to halla, a charge. Mohalla is usually taken as an organized column, like a company on the march. Either way, it's a festival of movement. Why would a Guru do that? Remember the times. Guru Arjan and Guru Tegh Bahadur had both been executed. The Khalsa was just a couple of years old. Sikhs remember that Guru Gobind Singh wanted a people who could defend themselves and others, and who weren't ruled by fear. So he took a season of play and pointed it at courage and skill. It's still a game and a joy, but it trains the body. Today the festival runs over several days. There's gatka, the Sikh art of stick and sword. There's horsemanship, much of it from the Nihang Singhs, in deep blue, who keep the old martial ways alive. There's kirtan, and gatherings of poets, as there were, tradition says, at Guru Gobind Singh's court. It closes with a great procession. Underneath is an idea you've met before: the saint-soldier. In Sikh teaching, devotion and strength aren't opposites; a body that can run, stand and protect belongs to a life given to the Name. Hola Mohalla puts that on an open field and lets it be fun. Strength, in joy, not in anger.
screen: `THE DAY AFTER HOLI, AT ANANDPUR.` · `HOLA — A CHARGE. MOHALLA — A COLUMN.` · `PLAY, POINTED AT COURAGE.` · `GATKA, HORSES AND POETRY.` · then, large: `THE SAINT-SOLDIER.`

segments.voice: Stand if you can, roll your shoulders back, shake out your hands, and march gently in place or step side to side; if you're sitting, sweep your arms slowly, like parting tall grass. Keep it light, a festival, not a workout, and let your breath keep time, with Waheguru riding on it if you pray. Enjoy whatever strength you have today, however much or little, then slow down and let the body settle.
Hola Mohalla. The festival of mock battles, gatka and poetry at Anandpur, the day after Holi, begun by Guru Gobind Singh.
Your line: strength, in joy. Strong and glad at the same time. Day one hundred fifty-two, done.
